title: 144 times a day
hook: 144 times a day; putting it face down is a practice

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: awareness. Your line: look at the looker. Did you ask it, even once, at a red light or brushing your teeth? What did you find? Day sixteen.

A hundred and forty-four. That's how many times a day, according to one survey of Americans, people check their phones. Spread over sixteen waking hours, it's about once every six or seven minutes. And where's yours right now? There's a decent chance you're listening to this on it. A lot of those checks don't feel like decisions. The hand just goes. Nobody here is going to tell you to throw it in a lake. It's how you talk to people you love, and it's how you got here today. But today's idea is small and a little radical: putting it face down is a practice. Today's word is the phone.
screen: `ABOUT 144 TIMES A DAY.` → `WHERE IS YOURS?` → `FACE DOWN IS A PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Remember Pascal from day two, who traced the unhappiness of men to one fact: "they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber"? He was writing about hunting and gambling and the busy royal court. He never saw a phone. But he'd recognize the reach of the hand. In 2017, researchers at the University of Texas ran a simple experiment. People did tests of attention and memory with their phones either on the desk face down, in a pocket or bag, or in another room. All phones were silent. The people whose phones were in another room did best. The phone didn't have to buzz. Just being nearby seemed to pull at part of the mind. So face down is a start, and the next room is even better. And there's an old practice that already knows this shape. In Jewish tradition, the Sabbath is a day each week when work stops, from sundown Friday to nightfall Saturday. The rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described it as a kind of palace built in time rather than in space: not a place you go, but a stretch of hours you protect. For Sabbath-observant Jews, the phone is set down with the rest of the week's work. Some people outside Judaism now keep what they call a tech sabbath, a weekly stretch without screens. You don't have to start with a whole day. Three minutes is a start. The point isn't that the phone is bad. The point is that the hand should be yours. Putting it face down, on purpose, is how you find out whose hand it is.
screen: `PASCAL NEVER SAW A PHONE.` · `ANOTHER ROOM DID BEST.` · `A PALACE BUILT IN TIME.` · `THE HAND SHOULD BE YOURS.` · then, large: `FACE DOWN, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you're not listening on your phone, put it face down now, or in a bag, or in another room. If you are, set it down, screen down, as soon as the bell starts. Then sit for about seventy-five seconds. Notice any pull toward it: the hand, the itch, the thought that something might be waiting. Just notice the pull, and let it pass, like weather. It'll still be there after the bell. The bell holds the time.
The phone. A tool you love, and a hand that reaches on its own, until you put it face down on purpose. Sixteenth word.
Your line: face down for three minutes. Once today, at a meal or with someone you love, turn it over and leave it for three whole minutes. Notice the pull. Day sixteen.

screen: `DAY 16 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOU'RE NOT THE ONLY ONE.`

howItsDone: Sabbath-observant Jews set phones aside from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall, and some people of other backgrounds keep a weekly tech sabbath or phone-free meals.

original.note: Hebrew, from Jewish tradition: Sabbath, from a root meaning to stop or rest. A day when work, and for many the phone, is set down.

notes: The 144-times figure is from a Reviews.org survey (2023; earlier editions gave other numbers, e.g. 96 in an Asurion 2019 survey). The index title uses 144; the script calls it 'one survey'. Confirm source and year.
Brain Drain (Ward et al. 2017): conditions were desk (face down), pocket/bag, or another room; phones silenced. Confirm description.
Heschel's 'palace in time' is paraphrased (The Sabbath, 1951, is under copyright).
Sabbath hours: sundown Friday to nightfall Saturday; many observant Jews refrain from using electronic devices. A Jewish Keeper may refine 'many observant Jews'.
Original Hebrew שַׁבָּת from root sh-b-t, to cease/rest; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: the teach restated Pascal with the modern poster paraphrase ('not being able to sit quietly in a room alone') that day two explicitly corrects; it now uses Trotter's 'they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber', quoted and sourced. Also: hook no longer opens 'Quick question' (day six opens 'Quick check'), now leads with the survey figure and shows the waking-hours arithmetic, and drops the internal label 'today's hook' and the unsourced 'most of those checks'; cut 'in the sixteen hundreds', 'gossip' (Pensée 139 names the court, not gossip), 'twentieth-century', 'many observant Jews' (now 'Sabbath-observant Jews') and 'people of many backgrounds have borrowed'.
